author: Shane Garry Acedera
title: "What happens if he doesn't do any of those three but still sells shoes?" - Nike built a backdoor into Michael Jordan's first shoe deal in case he flopped - NewsBreak
text: In 1984, Michael Jordan signed a life-altering shoe deal with Nike . That contract paved the way for the arrival of the Air Jordan shoe and, later, the Jordan brand, both of which made Mr. Air the highest-paid athlete of all time and the first billionaire player produced by the NBA. However, while the Swoosh brand gave Mike an offer that was too good to resist in '84, it still had to protect its interests. Because they would be paying Jordan an annual amount three times bigger than the largest shoe deal during that time, they had to make sure that Mike performed at a level commensurate with what they were paying him. Nike inserted a clause that could invalidate the final two years of the agreement if Jordan did not meet certain performance conditions. The provision stated that Jordan had to either win Rookie of the Year honors, make an All-Star team, or average 20 points per game within his first three years in the league. If he accomplished any one of the three, the final two years of his five-year deal will be activated. In hindsight, the stipulations were too easy for Jordan. But back then, nobody knew what Jordan's ceiling was. MJ's agent, David Falk, had to make sure what the clause meant to his client. "What happens if he doesn't do any of those three but still sells shoes?" David asked Nike officials during the pitch meeting. Nike told Falk that if MJ sold $4 million worth of his shoes during the third year of his deal, the final two years of his deal would be activated. So, MJ had to deliver either on or off the court. Related: "We only needed one more guy" - Patrick Beverley says the Clippers lost SGA because Kawhi thought he needed more help Although Nike already had the prototype of the Air Jordan 1, Jordan wore the Nike Air Ship to begin his NBA career. Finally, on November 17, 1984, in a game against the Philadelphia 76ers, Mike officially debuted the Air Jordan 1. After shooting 4-17 with his new shoe, he ditched it in favor of the Air Ship. It was back on MJ's feet on December 20, and he never took them off. When Nike released it to the market in the spring of 1985, it became a phenomenon. Originally, Nike projected to sell $3 million worth of AJs over the first four years. Instead, sales reached $70 million in its first three months, and after only one year, it made over $126 million. Meanwhile, Jordan averaged 28.2 points per game in his first year with the Bulls and easily won Rookie of the Year honors. Not only did he make the All-Star team, but he was voted to be a starter on the Eastern Conference squad. Mike also made the All-NBA second team at season's end. Later in 1997, Nike's Jordan business got so big that it needed to create a division called Jordan Brand to specifically cater to Jordan shoes and apparel. In 2024, Jordan Brand hit the $7 billion mark in revenue, making it Nike's top sales contributor for the year. Meanwhile, MJ is sitting pretty with a net worth of $3.5 billion, while Nike Founder Phil Knight is the No.62 richest man, according to Forbes. What started as a calculated risk turned into one of the greatest investments in sports business history. The Air Jordan line redefined sneaker culture, helped Nike dominate the market, and made MJ an icon.
